entry.title: Stick to the Status Quo
entry.summary:
While watching a LIVE 24/7: High School Musical 1 on YouTube this morning, I realized… “Stick to the Status Quo” is basically the unofficial anthem of everyone telling founders what NOT to do. It low-key feels like a startup founder experience in the Philippines. Everyone’s basically saying: “Ganito na yan.”
But… startups literally exist because someone didn’t follow that advice. A lot of Filipino founders don’t fit one box — and that’s the point. Tech founders who care about community impact. Creatives building real businesses. Innovators solving very local problems with very new ideas. The ecosystem doesn’t always know what to do with that, so there’s pushback. Breaking from the norm is uncomfortable — especially when resources are tight and the risk feels personal. But every meaningful startup in the PH started with someone asking, “What if we try something different?” So no, founders don’t stick to the status quo. question it. We remix it. We build anyway. And sometimes, that’s how real change starts — when we get’cha head in the game. twinks

entry.title: Fixing HDMI Audio Stuck at 100% on Hackintosh
entry.summary:
If you’re running a Hackintosh using HDMI audio, you might’ve hit a super annoying issue: 👉 Audio is always at 100% and can’t be controlled Source Jervi-writes article All of classic Hackintosh stuff: Tweaking EFI / OpenCore
Audio layout changes Patching AppleHDA Different framebuffer configs Nothing worked. HDMI audio volume stayed locked at max. Turns out the fix wasn’t in EFI at all. MonitorControl (yes, the app used for external display brightness) completely solved the issue. Once installed: HDMI audio volume became adjustable Keyboard volume keys worked macOS volume slider finally did something No EFI changes needed HDMI audio is tied to the display, and macOS treats it differently than normal audio outputs. MonitorControl hooks into display-level controls, which indirectly restores proper volume handling for HDMI audio on RX480.

entry.title: Claude Code costs up to $200 a month. Goose does the same thing for free.
entry.summary: The artificial intelligence coding revolution comes with a catch: it's expensive. Claude Code, Anthropic's terminal-based AI agent that can write, debug, and deploy code autonomously, has captured the imagination of software developers worldwide. But its pricing — ranging from $20 to $200 per month depending on usage — has sparked a growing rebellion among the very programmers it aims to serve. Now, a free alternative is gaining traction. Goose, an open-source AI agent developed by Block (the financial technology company formerly known as Square), offers nearly identical functionality to Claude Code but runs entirely on a user's local machine.
